issues.subcategory: Mismatch between repeated exposure claims and lagged design
issues.description: Mismatch between repeated exposure claims and lagged design: The abstract’s “repeated exposure” conclusion may be stronger than the design directly demonstrates. The analyses test lagged associations from weekly aggregated incivility exposure while controlling baseline levels; they do not directly model accumulation of incivility across multiple weeks or trajectories of chronic exposure.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.

issues.subcategory: Negative-emotion target is unclear in mechanism section
issues.description: Negative-emotion target is unclear in mechanism section: The negative-emotion mediator is somewhat ambiguous in this section. The text first frames it as negative affect directed toward the perpetrators of incivility, but then theorizes a broader affective state toward customers generally, including customers who were not the specific sources of the incivility. In the nursing context, where experienced incivility can come from patients and family members but the mediator is negative emotions toward patients, this distinction matters for the conceptual interpretation of the mechanism.
issues.quote:
Although negative emotions may occur in response to general workplace stressors, we examine the role of negative affect specifically experienced towards the perpetrators of the incivility (i.e., experiencing negative emotions towards customers).

Affective responses to work events can build over time to influence overall affective states at work (e.g., Carlson et al., 2011). Based on this, individuals who experience consistent incivility from their customers likely develop increased negative emotions towards their customers, even if some of the individuals they are interacting with are not the specific sources of the incivility.

issues.subcategory: The focal stressor briefly switches from patient to coworker incivility
issues.description: The focal stressor briefly switches from patient to coworker incivility: The section is otherwise about incivility from patients or customers, and Hypothesis 2 concerns experienced patient incivility. The switch to “coworker incivility” changes the source of the stressor and breaks the caregiving/customer argument. The surrounding paragraph, hypotheses, measures, and results all concern experienced patient incivility, so this wording misidentifies the core independent variable in this part of the theory development. This should be revised to “experiencing patient incivility” unless a separate coworker-incivility construct is intended, which the measures and hypotheses do not show.
issues.quote: Within the current study, we look specifically at the relationship between experiencing coworker incivility and experiencing a caregiving specific form of job burnout, compassion fatigue.

issues.subcategory: Construct boundary in compassion fatigue section
issues.description: Construct boundary in compassion fatigue section: The construct boundary for compassion fatigue is somewhat inconsistent here: it is introduced as a specific type of burnout, but then defined as a broader construct consisting of burnout and secondary trauma components. Because compassion fatigue is a core mediator, this ambiguity affects whether the later hypothesis concerns caregiving-specific burnout, secondary traumatic stress, or a composite of the two.
issues.quote: Service employees with caregiving responsibilities (e.g., healthcare or education) can experience a specific type of burnout called compassion fatigue. Caregiving employees have a duty to routinely care for others, in turn exposing them to others' suffering, high stress, and trauma, in addition to the typical emotional stressors associated with service jobs (Coetzee \& Klopper, 2010). Compassion fatigue was originally developed by Joinson (1992) as a term for caregivers who have "lost the ability to nurture" (p. 119). Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components, with employees experiencing compassion fatigue if they are experiencing either caregiving-related burnout or secondary trauma (or both of these simultaneously).

issues.subcategory: Compassion fatigue needs a sharper boundary from negative emotions
issues.description: Compassion fatigue needs a sharper boundary from negative emotions: The mediation logic treats negative emotions toward patients as a proximal affective response that leads to later compassion fatigue. This definition of compassion fatigue, however, includes affective content such as anxiety, irritability, aggression, and cynicism, which sits close to the negative-emotions mediator. The paper needs to draw the line more clearly: for this study, is compassion fatigue an enduring caregiver-strain syndrome distinct from momentary or target-specific negative emotions? A short paragraph distinguishing the constructs, and noting whether overlapping affective descriptors appear in both scales, would make Hypothesis 2 easier to interpret.
issues.quote: The burnout component of compassion fatigue relates to feelings of hopelessness, anxiety, irritability, aggression, cynicism, and difficulty in performing one's job effectively or dealing with stressors from work (Figley, 2002; Finzi-Dottan \& Kormosh, 2018) that are related to caregiving responsibilities.

issues.subcategory: Construct mismatch: Incivility and secondary trauma
issues.description: Construct mismatch: Incivility and secondary trauma: There is a construct-matching concern in this sentence: after defining compassion fatigue as comprising burnout and secondary trauma, the rationale here effectively treats compassion fatigue as a caregiving-specific form of burnout. The rationale linking patient incivility to compassion fatigue mainly supports the burnout/strain component of compassion fatigue, rather than the trauma-related part. That makes the hypothesized incivility-to-compassion-fatigue path stronger for burnout-related symptoms than for secondary-trauma symptoms, especially given that incivility is defined as low-intensity rudeness rather than exposure to patients' traumatic experiences.
issues.quote: Due to the persistent relationships between job demands, such as incivility, fatigue, and strain experiences (e.g., Bakker et al., 2014; Crawford et al., 2010), and the conceptual overlap between burnout and compassion fatigue, we believe this relationship will replicate with a caregiving-specific form of burnout (i.e., compassion fatigue).

issues.subcategory: Construct alignment in Hypothesis 2 mechanism
issues.description: Construct alignment in Hypothesis 2 mechanism: Construct alignment is somewhat loose in Hypothesis 2: experienced patient incivility is operationalized to include patients and patient family members/friends, whereas the mediator is negative emotions toward patients. The paper’s chronic-hassle logic can support generalized affect, but the indirect path still partly assumes cross-target transfer from family-instigated incivility to patient-directed emotions.
issues.quote:
Applying this to the current study, we expect that incivility experiences will be related to compassion fatigue experiences due to increased negative emotions towards patients over time:

Hypothesis 2: Experienced patient incivility is positively and indirectly related to compassion fatigue through negative emotions towards patients: higher levels of experienced patient incivility is associated with increased compassion fatigue due to increased negative emotions towards patients.

issues.subcategory: Patient acuity and workload are somewhat conflated
issues.description: Patient acuity and workload are somewhat conflated: The construct boundary for perceived patient acuity may need tightening. The theory treats acuity primarily as patient-based workload or intensity of required care, while the operationalization asks for the percentage of patients classified as severe; to the extent severity does not reliably capture nursing workload in the sampled settings, the moderation rationale is less direct.
issues.quote:
The conditional role of perceived patient acuity
Given the nature of caregiving roles, it is likely these employees experience multiple job stressors occurring simultaneously. The impact of stressors on employee health and well-being outcomes is frequently researched across multiple occupations (e.g., Bowling et al., 2015; Crawford et al., 2010). However, most studies examine the collective or independent effects of multiple stressors on an outcome. The way in which multiple work demands interact to either heighten or reduce stress reactions has been less frequently studied (Jimmieson et al., 2017). Part of the stressor-emotion model of CWB relies on the stressor being appraised and perceived as stressful. Work factors have been shown to influence employees' perceptions of stressors as being a threat and, within nursing, interpersonal interactions and high patient acuity are consistently rated as threatening to wellbeing (Qureshi, 1996). In line with the stressor-emotion model of CWB, it is likely that recurring incivility experiences combined with workplace stressors, such as increased patient-based workload, can lead to a higher likelihood that the incivility will be appraised as stressful and, therefore, associated with heightened negative emotions.

A common way in which workers within the healthcare industry quantify workload is by patient acuity. Patient acuity is defined as "a measure of the severity of illness of the patient and the intensity of nursing care that patient requires" (Brennan \& Daly, 2009, p. 1119).

issues.subcategory: H3 setup implies a broader moderated mediation
issues.description: H3 setup implies a broader moderated mediation: The rationale for H3 appears to blur first-stage moderation with a broader conditional indirect effect. The lead-in says the experienced incivility × perceived patient acuity interaction will lead to negative emotions and “ultimately” higher compassion fatigue, but H3 itself only hypothesizes moderation of the experienced incivility-to-negative emotions path. Given H2, this wording reads like a moderated mediation claim even though the formal hypothesis is narrower.
issues.quote:
When considering patient acuity as an additional workload demand beyond experienced incivility, it is likely these cumulative stressors may diminish psychological resources needed to recover. In a study examining the impact of multiple stressors and incivility experiences on burnout, the authors found that increased patient acuity levels, escalated caregiver shortages, and minimal programs that reduce or buffer incidents of workplace violence can combine to create an environment where
acts of incivility flourish (Clark \& Springer, 2010; Babenko-Mould, \& Laschinger, 2014). Therefore, we expect the interaction effects of experienced customer incivility and perceptions of patient acuity will lead to increased negative emotions towards patients and ultimately, higher levels of compassion fatigue:

Hypothesis 3: The relationship between experienced patient incivility and negative emotions towards patients is moderated by perceived patient acuity: Increased perceived patient acuity strengthens the relationship between experienced patient incivility and negative emotions towards patients.

issues.subcategory: The patient-acuity moderation rationale needs a direct appraisal argument
issues.description: The patient-acuity moderation rationale needs a direct appraisal argument: The cited discussion leading into this sentence mainly supports the idea that high-acuity environments may be more stressful, or may be settings where incivility is more common. It does not yet explain why the same uncivil behavior should have a stronger emotional effect when acuity is high. The moderation hypothesis would be better supported by an appraisal-based premise: for example, uncivil behavior during high-acuity care may obstruct time-sensitive work, consume scarce attention, or feel more threatening to effective caregiving than the same behavior in lower-acuity weeks.
issues.quote: Therefore, we expect the interaction effects of experienced customer incivility and perceptions of patient acuity will lead to increased negative emotions towards patients and ultimately, higher levels of compassion fatigue:

issues.subcategory: Prior evidence is described more causally than the paragraph supports
issues.description: Prior evidence is described more causally than the paragraph supports: The studies are summarized with associational language—“positively related” and “associated with”—but the next sentence says it is clear that incivility experiences “can lead to” enactment. That goes beyond the evidence as presented, especially since the paragraph then says the over-time mechanisms have not yet been examined. A more accurate bridge would be: “Together, these studies indicate that customer incivility experiences are associated with employee incivility enactment, with the timing and mechanisms depending on the study design.”
issues.quote: Looking specifically at customer incivility, customer-to-employee incivility is positively related to employee-to-customer incivility (Torres et al., 2017), and service events containing targeted verbal aggression from customer to employee are associated with employee incivility enactment (Walker et al., 2017). From this, it is clear that incivility experiences can lead to increased incivility enactment.

issues.subcategory: Reversed model name in H4 theory rationale
issues.description: Reversed model name in H4 theory rationale: The phrase “emotion-stressor model of CWB” appears inconsistent with the stressor-emotion model named elsewhere in the paragraph and throughout the paper. If the intended framework is Spector and Fox’s stressor-emotion model, this local reversal should be corrected to avoid implying a different model.
issues.quote: Affective and exhaustion reactions to incivility have been identified as mechanisms for the experienced-perpetration incivility relationships (Schilpzand et al., 2016). Unlike early proposals of the incivility spiral, revenge intentions and rumination-based negative coping behaviors following a workplace incivility experience, although occurring, are not helpful explanatory mechanisms for why experienced incivility is associated with future enacted incivility (Vahle-Hinz et al., 2019). From the stressor-emotion model of CWB, negative affective responses serve as mediating mechanisms for why interpersonal stressors, such as experienced incivility, are related to increased CWB perpetration (Spector \& Fox, 2005). Supporting this, Roberts (2012) applied the stressor-emotion model of CWB to incivility and found that negative emotions were one mechanism through which organizational stressors were associated with incivility behaviors. In addition, burnout and decreased energy have been identified as mediators in the relationships between experienced incivility and job outcomes (Giumetti et al., 2013; Rahim \& Cosby, 2016). Similarly, using the emotion-stressor model of CWB, Margulescu (2020) found that compassion fatigue was a predictor of CWB enactment.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction regarding participant contact
issues.description: Contradiction regarding participant contact: The recruitment description is defensible as referring only to initial outreach, but the procedure does not specify how participants were contacted after enrollment for later survey waves and compensation. Clarifying the distinction between initial recruitment and post-enrollment panel administration would improve methodological transparency.
issues.quote: For all recruitment strategies, participants initiated the contact and study procedures by clicking on the study link or QR code that was listed in recruitment materials (no participant emails were obtained or used during the recruitment process).

issues.subcategory: Full-time eligibility conflicts with the final sample description
issues.description: Full-time eligibility conflicts with the final sample description: This reads as if full-time employment was required for entry, but the sample description later says participants were employed as nurses “part- or full-time” and worked more than one shift per week. That distinction matters in a weekly panel because part-time status changes exposure opportunity, and this inconsistency makes it unclear whether part-time nurses were eligible or included, which matters for interpreting generalizability. Please clarify whether part-time nurses were eligible and retained. If they were, revise the inclusion-criteria sentence to match the analytic sample.
issues.quote: Information about inclusion criteria (working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse) and compensation were also provided along with the link to participate.

issues.subcategory: Attrition counts and retention rates do not match the reported wave sizes
issues.description: Attrition counts and retention rates do not match the reported wave sizes: The arithmetic needs correction. If participants who missed a wave were not invited to later waves, then the T4 count is the number who completed all four surveys; 468 - 450 = 18 participants were lost to missing time points, not 16 as stated later. The statement that n=16 people were excluded for missing time points does not fit these counts. The final N also points to 18: 450 - 78 = 372, which is consistent with the final N=372, whereas 468 - 16 - 78 = 374. The later retention rates should also be 99% when rounded to whole percentages, since 454/458 = 99.1% and 450/454 = 99.1%. Please revise the missing-time-point count and the T2-to-T3 and T3-to-T4 retention rates.
issues.quote: The sample size and retention rates between each measurement time point were as follows: $\mathrm{n}=468$ nurses responded at time 1; n = 458 responded at time 2 ( $98 \%$ retention rate between T1 and T2); n = 454 responded at time 3 ( $98 \%$ retention rate between T2 and T3); and $\mathrm{n}=450$ responded at time 4 ( $98 \%$ retention rate between T3 and T4).

issues.subcategory: Demographic percentages are not traceable to the reported N
issues.description: Demographic percentages are not traceable to the reported N: These percentages cannot be checked against the stated final sample of N = 372. For example, 96.64% of 372 is 359.5008, not a possible respondent count. The race/ethnicity percentages also sum to 100.61%, which suggests either different valid-response denominators or non-mutually-exclusive categories. The denominators or the amount of item-level missingness are not reported, making the sample description difficult to interpret as written. Please report each demographic as n/valid denominator (%) and state whether race/ethnicity categories were mutually exclusive.
issues.quote: The majority of respondents were female ( $96.64 \%$ ), with a mean age of 34.44 (SD $=5.49$ ) years. This gender distribution, although overwhelmingly female, is not atypical of the healthcare profession: around $76 \%$ of healthcare workers are women and, as of 2019, around $88 \%$ of registered nurses are women (Connor et al., 2020; U.S. Census Bureau, 2019). $74.55 \%$ of the respondents self-identified as White, $15.45 \%$ self-identified as Hispanic or Latino, $5.76 \%$ self-identified as Black, and $4.85 \%$ self-identified as Asian.

issues.subcategory: The item-selection rule is stated too broadly
issues.description: The item-selection rule is stated too broadly: This sentence implies that every measure in the study was shortened by selecting the highest-loading items. The measure descriptions do not support that: patient acuity is a new single item, compassion fatigue uses a 13-item short scale, and negative emotions is presented as a four-emotion scale. Narrow the sentence to the scales that were actually shortened, and then describe the selection rule for those scales only.
issues.quote: For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability (Maloney et al., 2011).

issues.subcategory: Part-whole correlations are not independent validity evidence
issues.description: Part-whole correlations are not independent validity evidence: These correlations are useful descriptive checks, but they are partly mechanical because the short form is included inside the full form. If the full score is F = S + O, where S is the short form and O is the omitted items, corr(S,F) is inflated by the shared S component. The text should present these as evidence that the short form overlaps with the full item set, not as independent validation that the shortened measure preserves the omitted content.
issues.quote: assessed part-whole correlations between the full scales and shortened versions during pilot testing ( $r$ (48) = .91, $p<.001$ for experienced patient incivility and $r(48)=.93, p<.001$ for enacted patient incivility)

issues.subcategory: Eigenvalues cannot justify item-level selection
issues.description: Eigenvalues cannot justify item-level selection: Eigenvalues summarize factor-level variance; they do not show how strongly each selected item loads on the factor. A factor can have a large eigenvalue while a chosen item loads less strongly than an omitted item. Since this sentence is part of the justification for shortening the scale, it should refer to item factor loadings, item-total information, or another item-level criterion. If only eigenvalues were checked, the claim that the selected items were “highly loaded” should be removed.
issues.quote: (d) examined the eigenvalues reported in the original scale development paper (Cortina et al., 2001) to ensure that the selected items are highly loaded onto the incivility factor.

issues.subcategory: Patient acuity measure may not be standardized
issues.description: Patient acuity measure may not be standardized: The patient acuity measure may not fully standardize the meaning of “severe” across departments and acuity systems. Because the percentage of “severe” patients is later used as a moderator, the paper needs a stronger basis for treating these responses as a comparable perceived-acuity metric across heterogeneous nursing settings.
issues.quote: Based on Brennan and Daly's (2009) findings that the judgement of severity is a key component of patient acuity, we measure the respondents' perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were "severe." To help standardize judgements of severity, we built our question around existing workplace patient acuity indicators (i.e., "based on your department's patient acuity scale..."). Because participants were all required to work within some level of critical care or high-stakes setting, they were asked to rate, "Based on your department's patient acuity scale (i.e., the measure you use to determine the severity of your patient's condition), what percentage of patients under your care in the past week would be considered "severe"? Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools".

issues.subcategory: Measures: Flawed operationalization of Patient Acuity
issues.description: Measures: Flawed operationalization of Patient Acuity: The patient acuity item raises measurement concerns. It lists patient-reported outcome assessment tools as examples alongside acuity or severity indices, although PRO instruments are not typically department-level acuity classifications. In addition, the moderated analyses appear to use a reduced sample because of missing or out-of-range acuity responses, which heightens concern about whether respondents interpreted the percentage “severe” item consistently enough for use as the key moderator.
issues.quote: Because participants were all required to work within some level of critical care or high-stakes setting, they were asked to rate, "Based on your department's patient acuity scale (i.e., the measure you use to determine the severity of your patient's condition), what percentage of patients under your care in the past week would be considered "severe"? Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools".

issues.subcategory: The enacted-incivility measure is attributed as a separate Cortina scale
issues.description: The enacted-incivility measure is attributed as a separate Cortina scale: Earlier in the measures section, Cortina et al. (2001) is introduced as the source of the Workplace Incivility Scale for experienced incivility. The next sentence here says the enacted items were similar to those items with the instructions changed, which reads as an adaptation rather than a separate original “Enacted Incivility Scale” from Cortina et al. To help readers trace the measure, describe these as items adapted from the Workplace Incivility Scale, following prior use for enacted incivility if that is the intended source chain.
issues.quote: Enacted Incivility. Four items from the Enacted Incivility Scale (Cortina et al., 2001) were used to measure the frequency participants instigated incivility towards their patients.

issues.subcategory: Causal-inference language overstates what the autoregressive model controls
issues.description: Causal-inference language overstates what the autoregressive model controls: Autoregressive controls and time ordering make the paths more informative than same-wave associations, but they do not rule out time-varying confounding. A simple example shows the problem: suppose workload U2 causes both T2 incivility perceptions X2 and T3 negative emotions Y3, with no causal effect of X2 on Y3. If X2 = U2 + eX and Y3 = U2 + eY, then regressing Y3 on X2 and prior Y still gives a positive coefficient on X2 because both contain U2. The methods section should say that the model adjusts for prior construct levels and improves temporal ordering, while causal interpretation still depends on unmeasured time-varying confounders and other bias sources being limited.
issues.quote: This method also supports a lower likelihood of third variable effects (Bliese et al., 2020; Cole \& Maxwell, 2003; Duncan et al., 2004) and allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time.

issues.subcategory: The Monte Carlo target is described imprecisely
issues.description: The Monte Carlo target is described imprecisely: For mediation CIs, the simulation approximates the sampling distribution of the estimated indirect effect or IMM, not a population distribution of respondents or construct scores. In practice, the estimated path coefficients and their uncertainty are drawn repeatedly, transformed into products, and the quantiles of those products form the interval. Revise the sentence to say that the Monte Carlo procedure approximates the sampling distribution of the indirect effects and IMM from the estimated coefficients and their standard errors or covariances.
issues.quote: The Monte Carlo simulation addresses potential imbalances in confidence limits by simulating a population distribution using the sample parameter estimates (Mackinnon et al., 2004).

issues.subcategory: CFA reporting in Analytic Strategy is hard to reconcile
issues.description: CFA reporting in Analytic Strategy is hard to reconcile: The CFA paragraph appears to mix or insufficiently label absolute model-fit statistics and chi-square difference-test statistics. The degrees of freedom reported for the three-, two-, and one-factor alternatives are not plausible as absolute CFA model degrees of freedom, while RMSEA, CFI, and TLI are reported alongside them as if they were ordinary model-fit indices. This makes the discriminant-validity evidence difficult to evaluate as written.
issues.quote: Before evaluating our hypotheses, we investigated the discriminant validity of our measures by employing a series of confirmatory factor analyses. First, we assessed our hypothesized four-factor model absent of the temporal control measures. We applied procedures recommended by Nye and Drasgow (2011) to model the data at the item-level using WLSMV in MPlus 8.0. The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable $(269)=862.05$, RMSEA $=.08$, CFI $=.99$, TLI $=$ .99) and fit the data better than a three-factor model wherein both incivility measures were set to load onto the same factor $(3)=82.52$, RMSEA $=.09$, CFI $=.98$, TLI $=.98$ ), a two-factor model wherein both incivility measures were loaded onto one factor and negative emotions towards patients and compassion fatigue were loaded onto the second factor (2) $=82.65, \mathrm{RMSEA}=.10, \mathrm{CFI}=.98, \mathrm{TLI}=.98$ ), and a one-factor model (1) $=8.02, \mathrm{RMSEA}=.10, \mathrm{CFI}=.98, \mathrm{TLI}=.98$ ).

issues.subcategory: Missing-data handling is unclear before Results
issues.description: Missing-data handling is unclear before Results: The missing-data discussion notes that perceived patient acuity had missing or invalid responses, but it does not state how many cases were affected or how missingness was handled analytically. This matters because the final sample is N=372, whereas the main mediation tables use N=321 and the moderation table uses N=244, apparently due to moderator missingness. Table 3 explains its smaller N as due to moderator missingness, but the reduction to N=321 for the descriptive correlations and main mediation regressions is not explained. Unless this reflects a clearly defined complete-case analytic sample or another missing-data decision, the discrepancy leaves the effective sample size for the main results unclear. The analytic samples and missing-data treatment should be clearer for interpreting the moderation and mediation results.
issues.quote:
Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank ( $55 \%$ of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range ( $45 \%$ of missing values were due to an incorrect response). However, a comparison of personal demographics and workplace characteristics did not find any significant differences between participants with and without missing values for perceived patient acuity.

## Results

Table 1 presents intercorrelations among study variables and descriptive information. An overview of the results, as they relate to our hypothesized model, can be viewed in Figure 2.

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis 2 indirect effect does not match the reported path product
issues.description: Hypothesis 2 indirect effect does not match the reported path product: The point estimate for Hypothesis 2 should match the product of the two displayed paths. The text reports .26 for T2 experienced patient incivility predicting T3 negative emotions and .37 for T3 negative emotions predicting T4 compassion fatigue. Their product is .096, which would round to .10; even with ordinary two-decimal rounding, this product cannot be .07. If the MPlus constraint used different coefficients, those coefficients need to be shown. Otherwise, revise the indirect estimate and its SE/CI from the same model. As written, readers cannot tell which mediation path was tested.
issues.quote: We then used MPlus' model constraint feature to estimate the indirect path $a \times d$. In support of Hypothesis 2, the positive indirect relationship between experienced patient incivility and compassion fatigue through negative emotions was significant $(\mathrm{B}=.07, \mathrm{SE}=.03, \mathrm{p}<.05,95 \% \mathrm{Cl}[0.02,0.14])$.

issues.subcategory: The Hypothesis 3 interpretation sounds like a main-effect claim
issues.description: The Hypothesis 3 interpretation sounds like a main-effect claim: This wording reads as if the hypothesis predicted a positive main effect of acuity on negative emotions. The test that follows is a simple-slopes analysis of experienced incivility predicting negative emotions at low, medium, and high acuity. Those are different claims. Rephrase this as a moderation statement: the positive relationship between experienced patient incivility and negative emotions was expected to be stronger when perceived patient acuity was higher.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 3 also predicted that the conditional relationship would be such that employees reporting higher perceived patient acuity would also report higher negative emotions.

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis 4 SE, p-value, and confidence interval are inconsistent
issues.description: Hypothesis 4 SE, p-value, and confidence interval are inconsistent: The reported inferential statistics do not line up. With B = .06 and SE = .04, the ratio is 1.50, which does not support p < .01 under the usual large-sample test, and a normal 95% interval would include zero. The stated CI [0.02, 0.10] instead suggests an SE closer to .02, which is also the SE shown for this indirect effect in Table 2. The estimate appears to be the same effect, so the standard error should be reconciled. Please correct the SE in the text if .02 is the intended value, or revise the p-value and confidence interval if .04 is correct.
issues.quote: As expected, Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients $(\mathrm{B}=.06, \mathrm{SE}=.04, \mathrm{p}<.01,95 \% \mathrm{CI}[0.02$, 0.10]).

issues.subcategory: Contradictory estimates in relative importance analysis
issues.description: Contradictory estimates in relative importance analysis: The supplemental-analysis paragraph appears internally inconsistent. The claim that compassion fatigue has a parameter estimate nearly six times that of negative emotions does not seem to match Table 2, where the enacted-incivility coefficients appear to be $B=.57$ for compassion fatigue and $B=.28$ for negative emotions. The subsequent $lm()$ results also report the same coefficient for negative emotions and compassion fatigue ($B=.23$), so the comparison and regression output should be checked or clarified.
issues.quote: As seen in Table 2 , the last step of the simple mediation reflects a parameter estimate for compassion fatigue that is nearly six times that of negative emotions. Because regression only provides information on how much scores a given outcome change following a single unit change in a given predictor, we conducted a relative importance analysis to understand the proportion of variance each predictor accounts for in enacted incivility (Tonidandel \& LeBreton, 2011). First, using the native $\operatorname{lm}()$ function in $R$ ( $R$ Core Team, 2021), we regressed enacted incivility on predictors from this stage--experienced incivility ( $\mathrm{B}=-.03$, $\mathrm{SE}=.04, \mathrm{p}=.40$ ), negative emotions ( $\mathrm{B}=.23, \mathrm{SE}=.04, \mathrm{p}<.001$ ), and compassion fatigue ( $\mathrm{B}=.23$, $\mathrm{SE}=.04, \mathrm{p}<.001$ ).

issues.subcategory: Dropped autoregressive controls in supplemental analysis
issues.description: Dropped autoregressive controls in supplemental analysis: The relative-importance analysis may not be directly comparable to the autoregressive mediation model. The description says enacted incivility was regressed on experienced incivility, negative emotions, and compassion fatigue, with no mention of the Time 1 autoregressive or work-hour controls used in the main analyses. If those controls were omitted, the reported 45.1%/30.8%/24.1% variance shares describe a different, less-adjusted model rather than the variance decomposition of the main longitudinal model.
issues.quote: Because regression only provides information on how much scores a given outcome change following a single unit change in a given predictor, we conducted a relative importance analysis to understand the proportion of variance each predictor accounts for in enacted incivility (Tonidandel \& LeBreton, 2011). First, using the native $\operatorname{lm}()$ function in $R$ ( $R$ Core Team, 2021), we regressed enacted incivility on predictors from this stage--experienced incivility ( $\mathrm{B}=-.03$, $\mathrm{SE}=.04, \mathrm{p}=.40$ ), negative emotions ( $\mathrm{B}=.23, \mathrm{SE}=.04, \mathrm{p}<.001$ ), and compassion fatigue ( $\mathrm{B}=.23$, $\mathrm{SE}=.04, \mathrm{p}<.001$ ).

issues.subcategory: Relative-importance shares should be described as explained variance
issues.description: Relative-importance shares should be described as explained variance: The three percentages sum to 100%, so they are best read as normalized shares of the model’s explained variance, not percentages of total variance in enacted incivility. If they were percentages of total outcome variance, the model would have R² = 1. Please revise the sentence to say that the relative-importance analysis partitioned the regression model’s explained variance, with those three predictors accounting for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of explained variance, respectively.
issues.quote: The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for $45.1 \%, 30.8 \%$, and $24.1 \%$ of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.subcategory: The discussion uses “partial mediation” without reporting the remaining direct path
issues.description: The discussion uses “partial mediation” without reporting the remaining direct path: “Partial mediation” has a specific meaning: the indirect path is present and a residual direct path remains after the mediators are included. The discussion sentence only states the indirect process, and the results text does not clearly report a remaining direct effect from experienced patient incivility to enacted incivility after the mediators. Either report and interpret that direct path, or change the wording to “an indirect process” so the conclusion matches the evidence shown.
issues.quote: Our results support a partial mediation process: in support of our hypotheses, experiencing incivility from patients was related to increased future incivility enactment towards patients indirectly through increased negative emotions towards patients and compassion fatigue.

issues.subcategory: “Negative relationship” is ambiguous in a path statement
issues.description: “Negative relationship” is ambiguous in a path statement: Here “negative” seems to mean harmful, but in a mediation-path discussion it can also mean a negative statistical association. The tested first-stage path is positive: higher experienced incivility is associated with higher negative emotions, and acuity strengthens that association. Replace “negative relationship” with “positive association between experienced incivility and negative affective responses” to avoid sign confusion.
issues.quote: Further, the presence of an additional job stressor (i.e., perceived patient acuity) exacerbates the negative relationship between experienced incivility and negative affective responses

issues.subcategory: Patient acuity is grouped with interpersonal stressors
issues.description: Patient acuity is grouped with interpersonal stressors: Patient acuity is not an interpersonal behavior in the way patient incivility is. Elsewhere the paper treats acuity as workload or a care-related demand, and the measure asks about the percentage of severe patients. The theoretical contribution is cleaner if the sentence says that an interpersonal stressor, experienced patient incivility, interacts with a task-related or care-demand stressor, perceived patient acuity.
issues.quote: Moreover, our results suggest that multiple environmental, interpersonal stressors (experienced incivility from patients and perceived patient acuity) interact to influence the way incivility stressors and strain relate to each other.

issues.subcategory: Confounded comparison of concurrent vs. lagged predictors
issues.description: Confounded comparison of concurrent vs. lagged predictors: The comparison behind the claim that compassion fatigue is a “stronger driver” of enacted incivility is confounded by timing. Compassion fatigue and enacted incivility were measured at Time 4, whereas negative emotions were measured at Time 3, so the relative importance results compare a concurrent predictor with a lagged predictor. This supports describing compassion fatigue as the stronger proximal statistical predictor in the model, but not as a clearly stronger causal driver than negative emotions.
issues.quote: Further, our results suggest that while the emotion response is an important proximal response to incivility experiences, the subsequent compassion fatigue response is a stronger driver of enacted incivility. This builds on the stressor-emotion model of CWB by adding additional clarity on the ways in which emotion responses are translating into workplace behaviors.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction regarding moderated mediation on behaviors in multiple sections
issues.description: Contradiction regarding moderated mediation on behaviors in multiple sections: The discussion appears to extend the acuity moderation beyond the supported path. Perceived patient acuity significantly moderated the path from experienced incivility to negative emotions, but the conditional indirect effect to enacted incivility was nonsignificant (B = .04, p = .15). Thus, claims that simultaneous incivility and high acuity increase risk of enacted incivility are stronger than the reported moderated-mediation evidence supports. This issue also appears in the abstract, the practice implications, and the final limitations, where the scope of the moderation is overstated to include downstream behavioral outcomes.
issues.quote: In addition, these processes can be exacerbated when nurses are also perceiving high patient care-related demands, suggesting that nurses are at increased risk of the negative emotional processes and behaviors when they are simultaneously experiencing interpersonal (i.e., experienced customer incivility) and task-related (i.e., perceived patient acuity) stressors.

issues.subcategory: Customer outcomes claim exceeds the measures
issues.description: Customer outcomes claim exceeds the measures: The customer-outcomes claim seems broader than the measures support. The study measured nurses’ self-reported enacted incivility toward patients, which is customer-directed behavior, but it did not directly measure patient/customer outcomes such as satisfaction, safety, well-being, or patient-reported treatment experiences.
issues.quote: Furthermore, although we use a healthcare specific population, our findings that incivility experiences from customers are negatively related to employee wellbeing (i.e., increased negative emotions and fatigue) are consistent with research using samples in other service sectors (e.g., Arnold \& Walsh, 2015). Examining perceived patient acuity as an additional workplace demand, the findings add to the literature that multiple demands examined simultaneously lead to harmful employee outcomes through the role of stress appraisals (Jimmieson et al., 2017). This adds to the generalizability of prior customer incivility research to further support that experiencing incivility from customers - even when the customers are patients, a population of people you have dedicated your career to care for - is associated with detrimental employee and customer outcomes over time.

issues.subcategory: Misattribution of inflated correlations
issues.description: Misattribution of inflated correlations: The discussion of inflated correlations appears to conflate two issues: limitations of future diary/ESM designs and the current panel’s very high bivariate correlations. The current study was a four-wave weekly panel analyzed with autoregressive mediation rather than a multiple-daily, person-mean-centered diary design, so the “within-focused nature” of diary studies does not clearly explain the present correlations. Table 1 also appears to show extremely high correlations among key constructs, including T4 compassion fatigue and T4 enacted incivility at about r=.94, which raises a distinct concern about empirical distinctiveness, common-method or stable between-person variance, and possible multicollinearity. A cleaner revision would say that future diary or experience-sampling studies could use person-mean centering or multilevel models to separate stable between-person differences from event-level covariation, without implying that a diary-design artifact caused the current correlations.
issues.quote: Additionally, diary studies of this nature may produce inflated correlations between variables within and across points in time due to the within-focused nature of the design (Beal, 2015). We acknowledge this particular issue in this study as some of the bivariate relationships are higher than convention. Future researchers may address this particular issue by integrating a latent multilevel framework that reduces potential serial and inflation effects by employing a within design that centers variables on the individual mean (Beal, 2015; Gabriel et al., 2019).

issues.subcategory: Repeated nurse-patient contact is ruled out more strongly than the data allow
issues.description: Repeated nurse-patient contact is ruled out more strongly than the data allow: The paper identifies repeated contact with the same patient as a possible alternative pathway, but then dismisses it too firmly. A handoff rate from “some nursing units” and a national mean length of stay for all hospitals do not establish the recurrence rate in this sample. The 6.1-day average is also close to the one-week survey interval and says nothing about the upper tail of patient stays. Nurses can have sustained interactions with the same patients or family members within shifts or across consecutive days. Since patient identities were not tracked, the safer conclusion is that repeated dyadic encounters could not be evaluated here; handoffs and work schedules may make them less common in some units, but they cannot be excluded. The argument would be more convincing if the transience claim were tied more clearly to the study’s weekly, future-customer focus rather than to customer interactions generally.
issues.quote: In combination with condensed 3 -day work weeks (Merrifield, 2017) and an average length of stay for all hospitals at 6.1 days (CDC, 2016), the likelihood that participants would be treating the same patients at multiple time points is very unlikely.

issues.subcategory: Implausibly high correlations indicating lack of discriminant validity
issues.description: Implausibly high correlations indicating lack of discriminant validity: The Table 1 correlation between T4 Compassion Fatigue and T4 Enacted Incivility appears to be very high ($r=.94$), raising a serious discriminant-validity and same-source/same-wave interpretation concern.
